summary: Specifies the Ad hoc On-Demand Distance Vector routing protocol for mobile nodes in ad hoc networks. It adapts quickly to changing links, uses little processing, memory, and network capacity, and finds unicast routes to destinations in the network on demand. It is an experimental specification.

plainLanguage.summary: AODV finds routes when a node needs to send data, rather than keeping routes for destinations that are not in use. Sequence numbers help nodes choose fresh routes and avoid routing loops.

questions: ad hoc on demand distance vector
how do ad hoc networks find routes
subtitle: On-demand routing for mobile ad hoc networks, with sequence numbers to keep routes loop-free.

tldr.problem: In a mobile ad hoc network, links and routes can change as nodes move. Maintaining routes to every possible destination would create unnecessary control traffic.
tldr.mechanism: A node broadcasts a Route Request when it needs a route. The destination or an intermediate node with a sufficiently fresh route sends a Route Reply back; Route Errors report unreachable destinations.
tldr.outcome: AODV is an Experimental protocol designed for mobile ad hoc networks whose nodes can trust one another. The RFC does not specify special security measures.

today: RFC 3561 is Experimental and does not specify an Internet standard. The RFC says AODV is designed for nodes that can trust one another and defines no special security measures.

sections.title: Routes When They Are Needed
sections.content:
The Ad hoc On-Demand Distance Vector (AODV) protocol provides multihop unicast routing among mobile nodes. A node does not need to keep a route for a destination until communication requires one. When a link breaks, affected nodes are notified so they can invalidate routes that use it.

Every route includes a destination sequence number. A node chooses a route with the greatest sequence number among alternatives, which the RFC uses to maintain loop freedom even when control messages arrive unexpectedly.
sections.plainLanguage: AODV discovers a route only when a node needs one. Sequence numbers show which route information is freshest and help prevent packets from following loops.

sections.title: The Four AODV Messages
sections.content:
AODV defines Route Request (RREQ), Route Reply (RREP), Route Error (RERR) and Route Reply Acknowledgment (RREP-ACK) messages. The message type values are 1, 2, 3 and 4 respectively. AODV sends its messages over UDP port 654.

An RREQ identifies its originator and desired destination. An RREP gives route information and a lifetime. An RERR lists destinations that became unreachable after a link break; an RREP-ACK confirms receipt when the reply requests acknowledgment.
sections.plainLanguage: AODV has a request, a reply, an error report and a reply acknowledgment. Together they let nodes find routes and report when a route stops working.

sections.title: Finding and Returning a Route
sections.content:
A node without a usable route broadcasts an RREQ. Each node that forwards it keeps a reverse route to the originator. The destination can answer, or an intermediate node can answer if it has an active route whose sequence number is at least as recent as the number requested.

The RREP travels by unicast along the reverse route. To limit network traffic, the originator should use an expanding-ring search: it starts with a limited IP time-to-live and increases it after a timeout. Repeated requests use binary exponential backoff.
sections.plainLanguage: The request spreads outward, and each forwarding node remembers how to reach the requester. A route reply follows those remembered steps back to the originator.

sections.title: Detecting and Reporting Broken Links
sections.content:
Nodes monitor the next hops used by active routes. They can use link-layer feedback, Hello messages or other methods to detect a break. A node then invalidates affected routes, updates their destination sequence numbers and sends an RERR to neighbors that may use those routes.

The RFC allows a node to try local repair for an affected route. It also defines route expiration and behavior after a node reboots, including a waiting period before it begins route discovery.
sections.plainLanguage: When a next-hop link fails, a node marks routes through it as invalid and tells affected neighbors. A node may try to repair a route locally before reporting it as unreachable.

sections.title: Trust and Security
sections.content:
The RFC designs AODV for networks whose nodes can trust each other, such as networks with preconfigured keys or no malicious intruders. It does not specify special security measures, even though routing protocols can be targets for impersonation.

Where the membership is known and attacks are a concern, the RFC says control messages must be protected with authentication. It identifies IPsec Authentication Header as an appropriate choice and recommends authenticating RREP and RERR messages.
sections.plainLanguage: AODV relies on trusted participating nodes and does not define security by itself. A network that faces attackers needs to authenticate routing messages.
